query: More than a century of research on conventional steels and other alloys has shown that exposure within certain temperature ranges can sharply reduce toughness and threaten safety in aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical applications. High-entropy alloys offer attractive strength, ductility, resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement, and wear resistance; however, their multicomponent chemistry complicates predictions of long-term mechanical reliability. Their resistance to rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation does not establish whether their toughness will remain stable after service-relevant heating, and this uncertainty limits engineering use. For a high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its as-designed condition, under the constraint that its original strength–ductility combination must be retained, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to reduce post-exposure toughness degradation? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to an otherwise identical untreated baseline, define the temperature, duration, and loading boundaries, identify supporting evidence from the observations summarized above, and describe a decisive experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a controlled amount of Zr to a high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloy will reduce post-exposure toughness degradation after service-relevant heating.
generation.material_initial_state: As-designed high-entropy alloy with original strength-ductility combination
generation.intervention: Addition of a controlled amount of Zr
generation.conditions: Service-relevant heating with temperature range between 500°C to 900°C, duration of 1-100 hours, and loading conditions of up to 80% of yield strength
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size refinement and solid solution strengthening due to Zr addition
generation.mechanism: Zr addition promotes grain boundary strengthening, reduces impurity-induced softening, and enhances thermal stability, leading to improved toughness retention after heating
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced post-exposure toughness degradation compared to the untreated baseline alloy
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy with original composition
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 500°C to 900°C, duration: 1-100 hours, loading conditions: up to 80% of yield strength
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Zr required for optimal toughness retention and the potential effects of Zr on other mechanical properties, such as strength and ductility

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the toughness of Zr-added and untreated high-entropy alloys after service-relevant heating using standardized toughness testing protocols
measurements: Microstructural analysis using TEM and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the toughness of the Zr-added alloy is not significantly higher than the untreated alloy after heating, the hypothesis is falsified

Origin of age softening in the refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions

Abstract: Most medium entropy alloys (MEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties, but their applications are limited because of their high density. This study explores a series of lightweight nonequiatomic Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs with a low density, high strength, and high ductility. To achieve solid solution strengthening, Zr with a large atomic radius was used. In addition, various thermomechanical treatment parameters were adopted to further improve the MEAs’ mechanical properties. The density of the MEAs was revealed to be approximately 5 g/cm3, indicating that they were lightweight. Through an X-ray diffraction analysis, the MEAs were revealed to have a single body-centered cubic structure not only in the as-cast state but also after thermomechanical treatment. In terms of mechanical properties, all the as-cast MEAs with Zr additions achieved excellent performance (>1000 MPa tensile yield strength and 20% tensile ductility).
